Virtually all the core falcons have a tomial 'tooth,' which is actually a notch in the cutting edge of the upper bill, and many of the forest falcons have bare facial skin, as do almost all caracaras. Falconids live most commonly in open habitats, from Arctic and alpine tundra to grasslands and shores; however, quite a few species, especially those in the subfamily Herpetotherinae, occupy dense forest. The diets of falcons and caracaras vary tremendously. Most falcons are strictly carnivorous, with some specializing on a single prey group (e.g., snakes in Herpertotheres). Many of the smaller species take primarily insects but will shift to small mammals and birds when feeding their nestlings. Most larger falcons take birds, usually while flying. Caracaras are more generalized, with many species taking a mixed diet of animals, both dead and alive, as well as grain and fruit. They, too, have species with interesting diet specializations (e.g., wasp adults and larvae in Ibycter). Most falconids are monogamous with biparental care, and, while most falcons nest in solitary pairs, there are some species that nest in large colonies, such as the Red-footed Falcon Falco vespertinus and Lesser Kestrel F. naumanni. Falcons use a variety of nest sites. Some, like the forest falcons and many smaller Falco kestrels, nest in abandoned tree cavities. Most larger falcons do not construct a nest, and instead use a cliff ledge or the unoccupied nests of other species, such as ravens, hawks, and owls. Most caracaras build their own stick nest lined with wool, dung, etc. Falconids lay 1 to 6 eggs, with 2 or 3 being the most common clutch sizes. The relatively large eggs are incubated for four to five weeks before hatching. In falcons, the female does the bulk of incubation, though both sexes participate in all aspects of parental care. The male does most of the foraging for the family, bringing food to the female at the nest, who broods the young until they are about a week to ten days old and partitions food to the nestlings, tearing bits of prey for the chicks to eat until they are strong enough to do it themselves. question: Based on the provided monograph, summarize the key family-level traits for the Phasianidae family, covering morphology, habitat, diet, breeding, and systematics as described.
answer: Family Profile: Morphology - Males often have brilliant plumage, feathered ruffs, wattles, airsacs, and crests due to intense sexual selection; females are typically plainer and handle all parental duties in polygynous species. Habitat - Terrestrial, found in diverse environments from Arctic tundra to tropical rainforests. Diet - Omnivorous, consuming leaves, seeds, berries, insects, invertebrates, and small vertebrates; some species like grouse are primarily herbivorous. Breeding - Diverse strategies including polygyny with lek displays (e.g., grouse), solo displays (e.g., Great Argus), territory defense (e.g., Common Pheasant), and monogamy; ground-nesting in shallow depressions with 4-20 eggs, precocial chicks hatching after 14-30 days, cared for by female or both parents in monogamous cases. Systematics - Sister to New World quails, with both groups sister to guineafowls; includes grouse and turkeys, previously often in separate families.

Phasianids live in pretty much all terrestrial habitats, from Arctic and alpine tundra to grasslands and deserts to humid tropical rainforest. Most phasianids are omnivorous, eating a wide variety of foods, including leaves, seeds, berries, insects and other invertebrates, and small vertebrates. Some such as grouse, however, are almost entirely herbivorous, taking insects only during the first few weeks of life. The various species within Phasianidae exhibit a wide diversity of breeding strategies. Many species are polygynous, with grouse famous for their lek displays involving many male contestants, peacocks and turkeys displaying in smaller groups, and some like the Great Argus Argusianus argus displaying solo to attract as many mates as possible. Other species, such as the Common Pheasant Phasianus colchicus, defend a territory with resources of value to females, and still other species are monogamous. The exaggerated plumages and displays of some phasianid males are meant to impress females, and they serve as excellent examples of sexual selection. Phasianids nest on the ground, usually in a shallow depression that is sometimes lined with dry leaves, generally concealed either under a bush or beside a rock. The number of eggs laid by a female varies widely among species, ranging from 4 to more than 20. The precocial chicks hatch after 14 to 30 days of incubation (longer in larger species). They leave the nest very shortly after hatching and remain with their parents (or just the female) to learn foraging techniques and receive protection. The female provides all the care in polygynous species. In monogamous species, the female incubates, but the male often helps tend the chicks. question: Based on the provided monograph, summarize the key family-level traits for the family Cinclosomatidae, covering morphology, habitat, diet, and breeding as supported by the text.
answer: Morphology: Resemble thrushes in shape with patterned, earth-toned plumage (jewel-babblers add deep blue), but have longer tails, shorter legs, and smaller heads, giving a sleek, low-to-the-ground appearance; songs are high repeated whistles, sometimes trills, with a strident quality. Habitat: Quail-thrushes inhabit dry woods, arid scrubland, and open arid plains, while jewel-babblers prefer dense, wet forests in New Guinea from lowlands to mountains. Diet: Primarily feed on small invertebrates and seeds, foraging on the ground by walking slowly, turning over leaf litter, and digging with bills; large insects are held down with one foot while picked apart. Breeding: Monogamous with biparental care, likely cooperative breeding; build simple, loose cup nests on the ground from grasses, twigs, and bark (jewel-babblers use palm fronds and jungle vegetation); females lay 1-3 eggs (typically 2), construct nests alone, and usually incubate alone (males may incubate in some species); incubation period is about 14 days, chicks leave nest after about two weeks, and both parents feed chicks (post-fledging care unknown).

Their songs are high repeated whistles, so rapid sometimes as to be trills, and often with the strident quality of the sound of grinding metal or insect calls. Quail­-thrushes mainly inhabit dry woods, arid scrubland, and open arid plains. Jewel-­babblers, by contrast, prefer dense, wet forests in New Guinea, ranging from lowlands well up into the mountains. Cinclosomatids feed primarily on small invertebrates and seeds. They typically forage on the ground, walking slowly while turning over leaf litter and digging in the soil with their bills. Large insects are held down with one foot while they are picked apart. Quail­-thrushes are monogamous with biparental care, likely with cooperative breeding. They build simple, loose cup nests on the ground from grasses, twigs, and bark. Jewel­-babblers, in their wetter habitats, use palm fronds and other jun­gle vegetation in their nests. Females typically lay 1 to 3 eggs, with 2 eggs being typical in most species. The female constructs the nest alone. In most cases, only the female incubates the eggs, although in some species, the male may also incubate. The incubation period is about 14 days, and the chicks leave the nest after about two weeks. question: Based on the provided text, describe the key family-level traits of the Cisticolidae family, including morphology, habitat, diet, breeding behaviors, and any notable conservation or systematic details.
answer: Morphology: Fine-billed, long-tailed, warbler-like birds; apalises are boldly colored and patterned, cisticolas are the most speciose. Habitat: Wide variety including tropical rainforests, arid shrubland, savanna, and freshwater marshes; require vegetative cover for foraging and nesting. Diet: Primarily insects and other invertebrates, occasionally small vertebrates, fruit, seeds, and rarely nectar. Breeding: Mostly monogamous with biparental care, some cooperative breeders; build ball-shaped enclosed nests with side entrances or open cups, often using grasses and plant materials, with some species stitching leaves together for protection; lay 1-7 eggs (typically 2-5); incubation 10-18 days (usually 12-15); both parents feed young except in polygynous species; nestlings fledge in 13-16 days, fed post-fledging for 2-3 weeks; among shortest generation times, breeding as early as 27 days after fledging. Conservation: 11% of species threatened (7 NT, 6 VU, 3 EN, 2 CR), with critically endangered species having restricted ranges. Systematics: Part of sylvioid radiation of oscines, separated into own family Cisticolidae; within family, four subfamilies recognized: Neomixinae (Madagascar endemic), Eremomelinae, Cisticolinae, and Priniiane.

provenance.source_chapter: Introduction, General Habitat, Diet and Foraging, Breeding, Conservation Status, Systematics History
provenance.exact_quote: Introduction These fine-billed, long-tailed, warbler-like birds reach their greatest diversity in Africa, with good numbers in Asia and very few in Australia. The apalises are the most boldly colored and patterned in the family, and the cisticolas are the most speciose. Cisticolas and their allies live in a wide variety of habitats, from tropical rainforests, to arid shrubland and savanna, and extensive freshwater marshes. Cisticolids require some degree of vegetative cover for foraging and nesting. Cisticolids feed primarily on insects and other invertebrates, occasionally taking very small vertebrates. Many species eat fruit and seeds occasionally, and it appears that some will also take nectar rarely. Most cisticolids are monogamous with biparental care, and some are cooperative breeders, with the helpers helping most in group territorial defense. Polygyny is known in at least a few species. Most cisticolids build ball-shaped enclosed nests with a side entrance near the top, and a few build open cups. Most nests are made of grasses, rootlets, moss, and other plant material, and at least one species fastens its nest by burrowing into a pendant clump of fibrous Usnea lichen. The tailorbirds, camaropteras, and several of the prinias and cisticolas have the distinctive and enchanting habit of enclosing their nests in adjoining large leaves, which are drawn and stitched together with spiderwebs, insect silk, or plant fibers to create a very durable protective shell for the nest. Female cisticolids lay 1 to 7 eggs, with most species falling in the range of 2 to 5. Nest-building and incubation are by both sexes or by the female alone. Incubation takes 10 to 18 days, 12 to 15 days in most species. Both parents feed the young, except in the few polygynous species, where males do not help. Nestlings are usually ready to leave the nest by 13 to 16 days after hatching, and fledglings are fed by the parents for at least two or three weeks after fledging. Cisticolas have among the shortest generation times of any bird, with some individuals known to begin breeding as soon as 27 days after fledging. Although many species of cisticolids face no immediate conservation concerns, forest conversion to agriculture compounded by small range size is a threat to 11% of species (7 NT, 6 VU, 3 EN, 2 CR). Both critically endangered cisticolids are restricted-range species. The cisticolas and their allies are part of the large sylvioid radiation of oscines. Previously allied with Sylviidae sensu lato, they were placed into their own family relatively early in the era of molecular phylogenetics (Sibley & Ahlquist 1990). More-recent phylogenetic studies have continued to support this separation of Cisticolidae, though its exact position within Sylvioidea is difficult to determine. Within Cisticolidae, we recognize four distinct subfamilies: Neomixinae, endemic to Madagascar, is sister to the remaining three distinct clades. Of the remaining three subfamilies, Eremomelinae is sister to Cisticolinae and Priniiane.

question: Based on the provided monograph, describe the key family-level traits of Corcoracidae, including morphology, habitat, diet, breeding behavior, and systematic relationships as detailed in the text.
answer: Family Corcoracidae exhibits high morphological divergence between its two species, both inhabiting mallee woodlands in Australia. They have a varied diet of insects, arthropods, seeds, and small vertebrates, foraging primarily on the ground. Both species are monogamous, obligate cooperative breeders with group sizes of 4-20 helpers, including both sexes, and build deep cup or bowl nests from mud and grass on broad horizontal branches. They participate in all parental care aspects. Systematically, they are part of the corvoid radiation of oscine passerines, with debated sister relationships to Paradisaeidae and/or Melampittidae.

provenance.source_chapter: Introduction, General Habitat, Diet and Foraging, Breeding, Systematics History
provenance.exact_quote: Introduction No other family of passerines packs so much morphological divergence into only two species. Though it would be hard to guess their sister relationship just by looking at them, both occur in the same mallee habitats of Australia, and both build bowl-shaped mud nests that are attended by bands of cooperative relatives. Their complex social lives are mediated vocally by a medley of ongoing chatters and chortles in the Apostlebird and shrieks and cries in the Whitewinged Chough (not to be confused with the corvids of the same name). The latter also adds a ventriloquial song, a high, ringing, descending whistle that can seem very far or close depending on which way the calling bird is turning. The corcoracids live in relatively open woodland, known in eastern Australia as mallee, from the tropics to the temperate zone. Corcoracids have a varied diet, consisting in the warmer months mainly of insects and other arthropods and invertebrates. They also forage on seeds, small vertebrates, and aquatic invertebrates. Both species spend much of their time foraging on the ground, and use their bills to forage through leaf litter and under branches and other material. Both corcoracids are monogamous, obligate cooperative breeders. Group size in these species ranges from 4 to as many as 20 helpers. As in most cooperatively breeding birds, the helpers are usually retained young from previous breeding attempts of the breeding pair. Unlike in other cooperatively breeding species, whose helpers are predominantly male, both young male and female corcoracids stay with the group. Both species construct a deep cup or bowl nest built of mud (with walls incorporating grass into the mud). Nests are usually placed on a broad horizontal branch. Nests can take several days to construct, and can be built at any time of year. Females generally lay 3 to 5 eggs. Both male and female members of the group participate in all aspects of parental care, including nest construction, incubation, and feeding young. Incubation takes 19 to 20 days, and the young leave the nest after another 18 to 30 days but are not fully independent of care from their parents and group members for at least another six months or so. Corcoracidae is in the corvoid radiation of oscine passerines. Despite their outwardly divergent morphologies, the two corcoracid have generally been placed together in the same family, based partly on their similar construction of mud nests; for the same reason, they were also often placed near the Grallina magpie-larks, which were sometimes considered a separate family, Grallinidae, but are now known to belong in Monarchidae. Corcoracidae is a “crown corvoid” family (Barker et al. 2004, Driskell et al. 2007, Reddy & Cracraft 2007, Irestedt et al. 2008, Jønsson et al. 2008b, Norman et al. 2009, Jønsson et al. 2011). Studies with extensive taxon sampling suggest that Corocacidae is sister to Paradisaeidae (Aggerbeck et al. 2014), to Paradisaeidae and Melampittidae taken as a clade together (Jønsson et al. 2011), or to Melampittidae alone (Reddy & Cracraft 2007).

question: Based on the provided monograph, what are the key family-level traits of the Cotingidae family, covering morphology, habitat, diet, and breeding?
answer: Morphology: Highly diverse in size (sparrow to crow-sized) and plumage (bizarrely colorful to cryptic), with auditory and behavioral elaborations due to sexual selection. Habitat: Primarily densely vegetated forests and woodlands, from lowland tropical rainforest to montane cloud forest, with some species in open scrubland and woodlands in temperate South America. Diet: Mostly frugivorous, feeding exclusively or almost exclusively on fruits, with some larger species including invertebrates, small frogs, and lizards; Phytotoma plantcutters primarily eat leaves, selecting high-protein ones. Breeding: Variable breeding systems including polygynous lek breeding with female-only care and monogamous biparental care; nests range from small cup platforms to large stick platforms or mud nests on rock faces; typically 1-2 eggs, with incubation 17-28 days and nestling periods 28-48 days, except Phytotoma plantcutters have shorter incubation (14 days) and nestling periods (17 days).

provenance.source_chapter: Introduction, General Habitat, Diet and Foraging, Breeding
provenance.exact_quote: Introduction No family of birds exhibits more diversity of auditory, behavioral, and plumage elaborations, all the result of rampant sexual selection, than do the cotingas. The species in this family vary in size, some as small as sparrows, others larger than crows. Some species are bizarrely colorful, others highly cryptic, with calls as divergent as the clarion calls of bellbirds and the calf-like mewing of the Capuchinbird. Males of many cotinga species group together in leks to display for females during the breeding season. In at least one species the lekking birds create their own forested habitat by regurgitating seeds that then germinate and grow up around them over the years of their traditional lek-site usage. Most cotingas live in densely vegetated forest and woodland habitats, ranging from lowland tropical rainforest to montane cloud forest. A few species, especially in temperate South America, extend into open scrubland and woodlands. Most cotingas feed exclusively or almost exclusively on fruits. A small proportion of the diet, especially of the larger species, includes invertebrates, mainly insects, and small frogs and lizards. The Phytotoma plantcutters feed primarily on leaves, and to a lesser degree on flowers and fruit. They appear to select leaves that are relatively high in protein. The breeding biology of most cotingids is extremely poorly known. Many species are polygynous with female-only care and lek breeding, though some are monogamous with biparental care. The nests of those that have been studied are variable. Many Pipreola, Xipholena, and Carpodectes species build a small cup platform of rootlets, lichens, and other plant material. Nests of the umbrellabirds (Cephalopterus) are usually large platforms constructed primarily of sticks. The cocks-of-the-rock (Rupicola) build a nest of mud and plant material that is fixed to a vertical rock face, sometimes in a shallow cave or other rock crevice. Females typically lay 1 or 2 eggs. In polygynous species, only the female provides any care to the chicks, constructing the nest and incubating the eggs alone. In monogamous species, such as the fruit-eaters, both male and female construct the nest; only the female incubates the eggs, although both male and female actively feed the chicks. Embryonic development rates appear very slow, and incubation takes 17 to 28 days. The chicks leave the nest after 28 to 48 days in the nest. The one exception to these slow rates of development appears to be the Phytotoma plantcutters, which have incubation periods of about 14 days and nestling periods of only about 17 days.

question: Based on the provided monograph, what are the key family-level traits of the Dicaeidae, covering morphology, habitat, diet, and breeding as described?
answer: Morphology: Small, brilliantly patterned birds with frenetic behavior and vocalizations including chip notes, shrieks, chatters, and twitters. Diet: Primarily feed on fruits and nectar, with some species eating seeds, insects, and other arthropods; many prefer mistletoe berries and play a key role in mistletoe seed dispersal. Breeding: Monogamous; nests are hanging pouches with side entrances, constructed of mosses, spiderwebs, and small roots by female alone or both sexes; females lay 1 to 4 eggs and likely incubate alone, with both parents provisioning chicks on a fruit diet; fledging occurs in about 15 days.

question: Based on the provided monograph, summarize the key family-level traits for the Emberizidae family, covering morphology, habitat, diet, breeding, and systematics as described.

question: Based on the provided text, summarize the key family-level traits of Fringillidae, covering morphology, habitat, diet, breeding, and systematics as described.
answer: Family Profile: Morphology - Diverse bill shapes from sharp and simple to massive seedcrackers, decurved probes, and uniquely crossed mandibles (e.g., Loxia crossbills), with wide color variation from streaky brown to brilliant colors. Habitat - Diverse, ranging from arid lowland scrub and savanna to dense tropical rainforests and high alpine talus slopes. Diet - Primarily seeds, fruit, and other vegetable matter; many species are nomadic, especially in Northern Hemisphere, searching for seed crops; some specialize in nectar, seeds, nuts, or insects (e.g., Hawaiian honeycreepers); nestlings are typically fed seeds or fruit, except Fringilla species feed insects to young. Breeding - Monogamous with biparental care; build open cup-shaped nests (except euphonias with dome nests) in trees, shrubs, or rock cracks; females lay 2-7 eggs, incubate alone; incubation 9-19 days, typically 12-14 days; fledging 10-27 days; post-fledge care up to two weeks in temperate zones or over a year in some Hawaiian species. Systematics - Part of superfamily Passeroidea within oscine passerines; sister to the large New World nine-primaried oscine radiation; includes three subfamilies: Fringillinae (sister to rest), Euphoniinae, and Carduelinae (with tribes including Drepanini, the Hawaiian honeycreepers).

provenance.source_chapter: Introduction, General Habitat, Diet and Foraging, Breeding, Systematics History
provenance.exact_quote: Introduction Fringillids vary widely, from the streaky brown of the European Twite to the brilliant colors of Neotropical euphonias, and from the sharp, simple bills of siskins to the massive seedcrackers of hawfinches and the chisels and decurved probes of Hawaiian honeycreepers. Yet this diversity masks some interesting shared traits. They are almost universally fond of fruits and seeds, so much so that even the nestlings are reared on them. Their mobility helps explain why they are the most widely distributed of all the nine-primaried oscines—and also why it is no big surprise that the spectacular diversification of Hawaii’s honeycreepers was seeded by a fringillid ancestor that colonized this isolated archipelago many millions of years ago. [GeneralHabitat] Fringillids live in diverse habitats, from arid lowland scrub and savanna to dense tropical rainforests and high alpine talus slopes. [DietandForaging] Most finches feed primarily on seeds, fruit, and other vegetable matter. Many, particularly those of cold Northern Hemisphere habitats, are nomadic, traveling large distances in search of good seed crops. Many Northern Hemisphere species are also quite specialized for different types of seeds. The Loxia crossbills are near the extreme end of this specialization, with uniquely crossed mandibles suitable for prying open conifer cones to extract the seeds. The Hawaiian honeycreepers, widely known for their diversity of bill shapes and sizes leading to strong feeding specialization, contain species specializing on nectar, seeds, nuts, or insects. Fringilla species feed their young insects, but the others feed their young seeds or fruit. [Breeding] Fringillids are monogamous with biparental care. Some nomadic species, such as Loxia crossbills, have been recorded nesting in all months of the year, and are limited only by the availability of conifer seeds for food. Others, such as the American Goldfinch Spinus tristis, nest relatively late in the summer, once their preferred nestling food, thistle seed, has ripened. Most fringillids build open cup-shaped nests of grass, twigs, rootlets, and other materials, most often placed in a tree or shrub, though alpine species place their nests in a crack in the rocks or under a cliff ledge, and euphonias build a dome nest with a side entrance. Nests of some species are often lined with feathers or plant down. Females typically lay 2 to 7 eggs, and euphonias lay large clutches for a tropical frugivore (2 to 5 eggs). Females generally build the nest and seem always, alone, to incubate. Across the breadth of environments these birds occupy, incubation can take as little as 9 days or as much as 19, but the eggs of most species hatch after 12 to 14 days. Nestlings fledge after about 10 to 27 days, and the young are cared for post-fledge for up to two weeks or so in the temperate zone and for more than a year in some Hawaiian species. In most species, both male and female feed the chicks. [SystematicasHistory] Fringillidae is part of the large radiation of oscine passerines known as the superfamily Passeroidea. Though one well-sampled molecular study suggested that Fringillidae is sister to Passeridae (Ericson & Johansson 2003), the vast majority of studies have indicated that Fringillidae is sister to the large New World nine-primaried oscine radiation (Yuri & Mindell 2002, Johansson et al. 2008b, Treplin et al. 2008, Fjeldså et al. 2010, Zuccon et al. 2012, Barker et al. 2013). Within Fringillidae, there are three distinct subfamilies: Fringillinae, consisting of only two species, is sister to the remaining members of the family (Lerner et al. 2011, Zuccon et al. 2012, Barker et al. 2013). Euphoniinae, which at one time was part of Thraupidae, is sister to Carduelinae. Carduelinae can further be broken into five tribes, including Drepanini, the Hawaiian honeycreepers, which at times have been separated into their own family (James 2004, Lerner et al. 2011, Zuccon et al. 2012).

question: Based on the provided text, describe the key family-level traits of the Grallariidae family, covering morphology, habitat, diet, and breeding characteristics as supported by the context.
answer: The Grallariidae family exhibits earth-toned plumage, long legs, and very short tails, with a body profile convergent on Old World pittas. They inhabit dense Neotropical forests across a wide elevational range, including above treeline for some species. Their diet consists of arthropods and other invertebrates, which they also feed to their young. Breeding is poorly understood, but they are thought to be predominantly monogamous with biparental care; nests are simple cups of plant fibers placed on branches or other supports at heights of 1-3 m, with females laying 1-3 eggs (typically 2), and both adults participating in nest construction, incubation, and feeding, though incubation lasts about 16-17 days and nestlings remain for 15-20 days.

question: Based on the provided monograph, summarize the key family-level traits for the Leiothrichidae family, covering morphology, habitat, diet, breeding, and conservation status as described.

question: Based on the provided monograph, summarize the key family-level traits for the Meliphagidae family, covering morphology, habitat, diet, breeding, and systematics as described.
answer: Morphology: Most have at least slightly decurved bills, with common ornamentation of brilliantly colored skin or feather tufts on the head and upper breast; brush-tipped tongues for nectar feeding. Habitat: Wide variety including arid scrubland, woodlands, tropical rainforests in Australo-Papua, where flowering plants are present. Diet: Specialized for nectar and pollen, but varied diet including insects, arthropods, fruit, and honeydew; many species are nomadic and territorial around nectar sources. Breeding: Generally monogamous with biparental care; some species breed cooperatively or nest colonially; nests are cup-shaped, hung from branches or in forks; clutch size 1-4 eggs; female builds nest and incubates, male and helpers feed chicks; incubation 12-17 days, nestling period 11-20+ days; post-fledging care lasts 4-6 weeks. Systematics: Rooted within Passeri as part of the meliphagoid clade, likely sister to Pardalotidae and Acanthizidae; includes Australian chats (Epthianura) but excludes Hawaiian Moho and Chaetoptila (now in Mohoidae).

Many of the Australian species have evolved complicated and poorly understood movement patterns, tracking the blooming of specific flowering plants over the vast expanses of that island continent. Most have bills that are at least slightly decurved, with ornamentation of brilliantly colored skin or feather tufts very common on the head and upper breast. Meliphagids live in a wide variety of habitats where flowering plants are present, from arid scrubland and woodlands in the Australian interior to the tropical rainforests of coastal Australia and New Guinea. Although honeyeaters have specializations of the tongue and bill for feeding on nectar, most have a very varied diet that also includes insects, other arthropods, and fruit, along with the honeydew secretions of insects. Many species are at least partially nomadic and will travel some distance to find sources of nectar. Many species are also extremely territorial and will vigorously defend reliable sources of pollen and nectar from other birds. Meliphagids are, with few exceptions, monogamous with biparental care, and some Manorina and Melithreptus species breed cooperatively. Some species aggregate to nest in colonies or, especially in Manorina, an expanded collection of territories with complicated and extensive interactions among other nesting pairs in the group. Nests are cup-shaped, and are either hung by the rim from branches in trees or placed in the fork of a branch. Meliphagids lay 1 to 4 eggs, with smaller average clutch sizes in tropical species. In most species, it appears that only the female builds the nest and incubates the eggs, but the male (and helpers, if present) helps in feeding chicks. Incubation takes 12 to 17 days, and nestling periods range from 11 to more than 20 days. The young seem generally to receive care after fledging, and in the few studies available, it appears that they become independent of parental care four to six weeks after fledging. The honeyeaters are the namesake of the meliphagoid clade, which roots deeply within Passeri. Within this clade, Meliphagidae is most likely sister to a group formed by Pardalotidae and Acanthizidae. Molecular phylogenetic studies have recently shown that the Australian chats (Epthianura)—a group of very brightly colored birds found in the arid lands of Australia that was often placed in its own family, Epthianuridae—fall within this family.

question: Based on the provided text, summarize the key family-level traits for the Motacillidae family, covering morphology, habitat, diet, and breeding as described.
answer: Morphology: Thin, long-tailed birds with long claws on the hallux, often with muted brown (pipits), gray/black/white with yellow (wagtails), or brown with yellow/red splashes (longclaws), and white outer tail feathers; most constantly pump their tails. Habitat: Primarily open habitats like grasslands, tundra, and savanna, with a few in wooded areas. Diet: Primarily insectivorous, also eating spiders, worms, crustaceans, snails, and small vertebrates; forage on ground and in air; supplement with seeds and berries when insects are scarce. Longclaws combine the browns of one with the yellow (or even red) splashes of the other, and they bear an uncanny resemblance to the meadowlarks (Icteridae) of the New World, in appearance and in their melodious whistled songs. They all share the white outer tail feathers so characteristic of birds of open country. Although only the wagtails translate the meaning of their family’s Latin name (Motacilla means “moving tail”), most motacilids constantly pump their long tails as they walk. Most motacillids are birds of open habitats, including grasslands, tundra, and savanna, though a few species live in more-wooded habitats. Motacillids are primarily insectivorous, often adding to their diet spiders and worms, as well as small crustaceans, snails, and even small vertebrates when feeding near water. Birds forage primarily on the ground, picking prey off the ground as well as making short flights to catch insects in the air. When insects are scarce, many species also feed on seeds and berries. Pipits, wagtails, and longclaws are primarily monogamous with biparental care, though both polyandry and polygyny have been observed rarely in well-studied species. Most construct a cup-shaped nest of grasses, rootlets, leaves, and other materials, which is well-hidden on the ground beneath a bush or nestled within a tussock. Many species place the nest in a hollow that they excavate or in the hoof print of a mammal. Females typically lay 2 to 6 eggs. Nest construction responsibilities vary, with both the male and female participating in some species, and only the female in others. Incubation, too, is by both sexes or by the female alone, and it takes from 11 to 14 days. Both parents feed the chicks, and the chicks leave the nest after 11 to 14, and occasionally up to 17 days. Care of the fledged young usually lasts more than two weeks and sometimes up to eight weeks post-fledge.

question: Based on the provided monograph, summarize the key family-level traits for the Muscicapidae family, covering aspects such as morphology, habitat, diet, breeding, and systematics as described.
answer: Family Profile: Muscicapidae (Old World flycatchers and chats) - Morphology: Upright-postured birds, often with dorso-ventrally flattened bills in some species, lighter build and more delicate legs than Turdidae, plumage ranges from earthtoned or black-and-white to blue spectrum. Habitat: Vast array including forest, grassland, scrubland, savanna, desert, and Arctic tundra. Diet: Mostly insects and other invertebrates, caught mid-air, gleaned, or pounced; berries and seeds significant in some species. Breeding: Primarily monogamous with biparental care, some polygynous or cooperative breeding; nests are open cups or globes of plant fibers and moss, placed variably (cavities, ground, trees); clutch size 2-8 eggs, incubation 11-18 days, chicks fledge after 10-18 days, post-fledging care up to 10 weeks. Systematics: Part of muscicapoid radiation in oscine passerines, sister family to Turdidae, with four subfamilies (Muscicapinae, Saxicolinae, Cossyphinae, Niltavinae).

provenance.source_chapter: Introduction, General Habitat, Diet and Foraging, Breeding, Systematics History
provenance.exact_quote: Introduction The Old World flycatchers at the core of this group are upright-postured birds, a surprising number of which catch their prey by gleaning or pouncing on insects on the ground as well as sallying into mid-air. Although some have the dorso-ventrally flattened bills that we associate with flycatching in other flycatchers, most do not. Many species in this family come in the form of plucky little ground birds, most of which are lighter of build and more delicately proportioned in the legs than are the Turdidae. Scattered across this group of largely earthtoned or black-and-white birds are species representing the entire spectrum of blue plumages, from a pale teal to the most intense iridescent sapphire. The Old World flycatchers and chats live in a vast array of habitats, including forest, grassland, scrubland, savanna, desert, and Arctic tundra. Muscicapids feed mostly on insects and other invertebrates. In many species, especially the flycatchers, insect prey is most often caught in mid-air, although most species also take prey while gleaning from branches or by pouncing on terrestrial prey from a perch above. In quite a few species, berries and seeds are a significant part of their diet. Muscicapids are primarily monogamous with biparental care. Some species are polygynous, with males mating with up to three females. Cooperative breeding is also known in a few species, with a single nesting female and up to several helpers that assist with nest-building and chick provisioning. Muscicapid nests are typically open cups or, less commonly, globes, built of various plant fibers and twigs and very often including a great deal of moss. Nest placement is highly variable; some species are obligate cavity-nesters or adopters of abandoned nests of other species, whereas others build their nests on the ground or in trees. Females typically lay 2 to 8 eggs, with smaller clutches in the tropical species. In many species, the female constructs the nest alone and is solely responsible for incubation, but in others, both sexes incubate. Incubation takes 11 to 18 days, and chicks leave the nest after 10 to 18 days of being cared for there. Both male and female are active in feeding the chicks, and the fledglings are fed by the parents for a week to ten weeks post-fledging. The Old World flycatchers and chats are part of the muscicapoid radiation of the oscine passerines. They are closely allied to Turdidae, and although these two groups have at times been merged together into Muscicapidae (Sibley & Ahlquist 1990), recent molecular analyses show that Muscicapidae is the strongly supported sister family to Turdidae (Barker et al. 2004, Cibois & Cracraft 2004, Zuccon et al. 2006, Johansson et al. 2008b, Treplin et al. 2008, Sangster et al. 2010). These two families together are sister to Cinclidae (Barker et al. 2004, Cibois & Cracraft 2004, Fuchs et al. 2006b, Zuccon et al. 2006, Reddy & Cracraft 2007, Johansson et al. 2008b, Treplin et al. 2008). Within Muscicapidae, there are four main clades that are recognized as subfamilies: Muscicapinae is sister to the remaining three groups. Of the three remaining subfamilies, Saxicolinae is sister to Cossyphinae, and these taken together are in turn sister to Niltavinae (Sangster et al. 2010, Zuccon & Ericson 2010).

Breeding is monogamous and cooperative, with groups of up to seven helpers; nests are cup- or tube-shaped, built of shredded bark, fur, and plant down secured by spiderwebs, decorated with bark and lichen for camouflage, placed in vertical forks of branches, typically with 2-3 eggs, incubated only by the female, with all group members feeding the young.

provenance.exact_quote: These short-tailed, light-limbed songbirds commute up and down branches and treetrunks in a series of short hops in a manner that recalls nuthatches (Sittidae) of the Northern Hemisphere. Yet they move with an agility and lightness of grip that their Northern Hemisphere counterparts lack, and, with bills that are thinner and less substantial than those birds of the north, they seldom, if ever, crack seeds. The sittellas occupy a variety of forested and woodland habitats, ranging from montane rainforest in New Guinea to more arid acacia scrubland and open woodland. The sittellas are primarily insectivorous, consuming particularly large numbers of insect larvae. They move up and down tree trunks and branches in search of their insect prey, gleaning them from the branch surface or from furrows in bark, and sometimes from foliage; occasionally they sally after a passing insect. Sittellas prefer eucalyptus trees with stringy bark for foraging, and there is anecdotal evidence that they use tools to extract larvae from trees. The sittellas are monogamous and breed cooperatively, in groups that contain up to seven helpers. They also are occasionally plural breeders, with two pairs in a group having separate nests in a large group territory, the young in both nests attended by all group members. And in some cases, two females will lay in the same nest, even incubating side-by-side. Sittella nests are cup- or tube-shaped structures built primarily of shredded bark with smaller amounts of fur and plant down secured together by spiderwebs. Nests are typically placed in the vertical fork of a branch, usually a dead one, and are decorated on the outside with flakes of bark and lichen, making them extremely well-camouflaged. question: Based on the provided monograph, what are the key family-level traits of Oreoicidae in terms of morphology, habitat, diet, and breeding?

provenance.exact_quote: Introduction Nowhere is the tremendous creative potential of sexual selection better displayed than by this family of songbirds endemic to the wet forests of New Guinea and northeastern Australia. Females are invariably clothed in earth tones, often with black barring, and most possess a strong, slightly decurved bill. Their uniformity makes the males that much more astonishing. Some have feathers in springy coils, others have profuse antennae on the rump, and still others have long breezy banners hanging from their napes. Incorporating this spectacular diversity of feathers into their displays with seemingly endless creativity, these males become feathered dancers, bizarre wind-up toys, or touchy-feely trunk creepers in their efforts to attract a mate. [DietandForaging] Paradisaeids feed on many different foods. Some species are exclusively frugivorous, taking an array of fruits and berries or, in some cases, specializing on figs. Many other species incorporate insects and other arthropods into their diet. The Epimachus sicklebills, with their long, thin, decurved bills, forage for insects in bark crevices and in dead and rotting wood. [Breeding] Most paradisaeids are polygynous with female-only parental care, but a few species, such as the manucodes and Paradise Crow Lycocorax pyrrhopterus, are socially monogamous. Particularly in polygynous species, males perform elaborate and highly stereotyped courtship displays. The type of display varies substantially among species, and display behaviors have evolved to show off specialized plumes and iridescent plumage patches and brightly colored skin in bizarre and exaggerated fashion. Many of the polygynous birds-of-paradise practice lek or dispersed lek breeding, in which males gather at specific sites that females may visit in order to compare the display quality of multiple males at one time. Nests of birds-of-paradise are either suspended loose cups or bulky cups constructed of stems, ferns, mosses, and other vegetation. Manucodes construct smaller, shallower, suspended cup nests. Females lay 1 to 3 eggs, most frequently 1 or 2. Only in the monogamous manucodes and Paradise Crow do males help with the breeding effort; otherwise, females of polygynous species undertake all nest-building, incubation, and chick-feeding responsibilities. Incubation takes about 14 to 27 days, and nestlings are in the nest for 14 to 30 days, both periods tending to be longer in more montane species. It appears that fledglings may be fed by their mother for up to three months or so after fledging. [SystematicasHistory] Paradisaeidae is in the corvoid radiation of oscine passerines, part of the 'crown corvoids' (Barker et al. 2004, Driskell et al. 2007, Reddy & Cracraft 2007, Irestedt et al. 2008, Irestedt & Ohlson 2008, Norman et al. 2009).

question: Based on the provided monograph, summarize the key family-level traits for the Paridae family, covering morphology, habitat, diet, breeding, and systematics as described.
answer: Morphology: Stouter bills adapted for seed-eating, with some species showing crests, masks, bibs, and varied colors. Habitat: Primarily forested habitats from boreal to tropical, requiring cavities for nesting, with some in desert scrub or arid areas. Diet: Insects as primary food, switching to seeds, buds, and fruit in colder regions; includes food hoarding and bill adaptations for seed-cracking. Breeding: Generally monogamous, with some cooperative breeding; cavity-nesters (often in trees or rodent burrows), laying 2-13 eggs (more in northern latitudes), with female incubation and both parents provisioning young. Systematics: Oscine passerines in superfamily Sylvioidea, near base of sylvioid radiation, often sister to Remizidae, with uncertain placement relative to other groups.

provenance.exact_quote: Introduction These familiar birds of Northern Hemisphere forest habitats have somewhat stouter bills and eat more seeds during the harsh winter months than do many other small passerine birds that resemble them. They reach their highest diversity in the Himalayas, where species display the entire array of crests, masks, bibs, and colors exhibited by this family around the world. Active members of mixed-species flocks in the non-breeding season, they are mostly monogamous hole-nesters, and among their ranks are the species with the largest clutch sizes of all the passerines. Most tits live in forested habitats, from boreal coniferous forests in the north to humid tropical forests in the south, but a small number occupy desert scrub and other arid habitats. Wherever they live, they require the presence of cavities to nest in; however, some will use holes in the ground. All tits feed on insects, and those in colder regions will readily switch from insects to seeds, buds, and fruit when insects are scarce. During the autumn, tits and chickadees that experience cold, harsh winters often hoard food for consumption later in the winter. When dealing with a large seed, a tit usually holds it with one foot and hammers it with its bill until it has accessed the rich seed inside. In years when many large seeds are eaten, this repeated hammering produces growth adjustments in the bill that make it thicker and a better nutcracker. Tits and chickadees are generally monogamous, with cooperative breeding in some Baeolophus species, in the African Parus species, and in Pseudopodoces. All nest in cavities, and almost exclusively in trees. Many use only cavities excavated by other birds (e.g., woodpeckers), although some will excavate their own cavities if the tree is already softened by decay. At least some parid species (White-browed Tit Poecile superciliosus and Ground Tit Pseudopodoces humilis) nest in abandoned rodent burrows. Most tits and chickadees line the inside of the cavity with moss and hair. Parids lay 2 to 13 eggs, with those in the northern latitudes laying many more than those in the tropics. Large clutches in the north are timed to capitalize on the peak abundance of insect larvae. When excavating a nest, both members of a pair will participate, but only the female generally builds the nest. Incubation is mostly or entirely by the female, and it takes 12 to 14 days (rarely up to 18 in far-northern species). Both parents provision the young, and the chicks are in the nest for 16 to 22 days before they fledge. Paridae appears most often to be sister to Remizidae, and these two taken together may be sister to Stenostiridae (Barker et al. 2004, Beresford et al. 2005, Alström et al. 2013a) or to Hyliotidae (Barker 2014).

question: Based on the provided monograph, summarize the key family-level traits for Passerellidae, covering morphology, habitat, diet, and breeding as supported by the text.

Breeding is generally monogamous with biparental care, involving open cup or domed nests placed in trees, shrubs, or on the ground, with females primarily constructing nests and incubating eggs (1-7 eggs, incubation 12-15 days, nestling period 7-15 days).

The New World sparrows live in a broad array of terrestrial habitats, from boreal muskeg to lowland rainforest, marsh to grassland, desert scrub to tundra, and savanna. Passerellids in temperate regions feed on a variety of invertebrates, fruit, and seeds, the last especially during the non-breeding season, and the relative proportions of seeds/fruit vs. insects vary greatly among species. question: Based on the provided monograph, summarize the key family-level traits of Passeridae, covering morphology, habitat, diet, and breeding as supported by the text.
answer: Morphology: Plain-clothed, sturdy little birds with special modifications of the palate and tongue for husking seeds. Habitat: Open habitats including agricultural fields, grasslands, savanna, desert, semi-desert scrub, open woodland, coastal pans, and alpine tundra; many species are commensals with humans in villages, urban areas, and farmland. Diet: Primarily granivorous, supplementing with insects, especially during breeding; chicks are fed insects and other invertebrates. Breeding: Monogamous with biparental care, strong pair bonds, often colonial nesting in cavities, abandoned nests, rock crevices, or burrows; nests are domed structures of woven grass, stems, and feathers; lay 3 to 5 eggs with incubation of 10-14 days and fledging after 13-17 days.

Still, passerids have special modifications of the palate and tongue with which they husk the many seeds they ingest. Granivory enables them to endure in some of the most extreme desert and alpine environments in the world. The Old World sparrows live in open habitats, from agricultural fields and grasslands, savanna, desert, and semi-desert scrub through open woodland, and from coastal pans to alpine tundra. Several of the Passer sparrows tolerate human activity extremely well and are often found as commensals in villages, urban areas, and farmland. Most of the Old World sparrows are primarily granivorous. Some species rely more heavily on insects than others, and all species feed insects and other invertebrates to their chicks. Old World sparrows are monogamous with biparental care. Pairs form strong pair bonds, and in some cases remain paired through multiple breeding seasons. Most species nest at least semi-colonially, and often in dense colonies, with the degree of coloniality depending on the availability of nest sites. The Passer sparrows nest most often in cavities or abandoned closed nests. The high-altitude snowfinches nest in rock crevices, and groundsparrows nest in burrows in the ground originally dug by small mammals. The nest itself is similar across most species, being a domed structure of woven grass, stems, feathers, and other items.

question: Based on the provided monograph, what are the key morphological, habitat, dietary, and breeding traits that characterize the Pellorneidae family?
answer: Morphology: Long-legged, short-tailed birds with earth-toned plumage (light beneath, often with crown/mask patterns); simple repertoire of high whistled songs. Habitat: Various forest types with dense undergrowth, from high-elevation to lowland tropical rainforest. Diet: Primarily insects, spiders, worms, and snails, mostly foraged on ground or in leaf litter; some gleaning from vegetation; berries/seeds minor. Breeding: Monogamous with biparental care (some cooperative breeding in Illadopsis); diverse nest structures (open cups to domed nests) made of leaves, twigs, moss; nests concealed on ground or low vegetation; 2-5 eggs; incubation 10-15 days; fledging 10-14 days; post-fledging care up to 9 weeks.

The ground babblers live in a variety of forest types, usually with dense undergrowth, ranging from cooler, high-elevation forests to low-elevation tropical rainforest. question: Based on the provided monograph, describe the key family-level traits of the Petroicidae, covering morphology, habitat, diet, breeding, and systematics as supported by the text.
answer: Morphology: Compact shapes with large round heads; plumages of grays, browns, and blacks above, contrasting with yellow, red, or pink underparts; some species have long tails cocked over backs. Habitat: Various wooded habitats including tropical rainforest, arid woodland, desert scrub, and edge habitats near fields and grasslands, from sea level to high mountains. Diet: Primarily insectivorous, with some species taking crabs, small vertebrates, or fruit; most pounce on ground prey from low perches, while others sally or glean from vegetation; scrub- and ground-robins forage mainly on the ground. Breeding: Monogamous with biparental care; long-term pair bonds; some cooperative breeders with helpers; nest shape variable (e.g., flat saucers, open cups, large bowls on ground or in forks); females lay 1-3 eggs (up to 6 recorded); females build nests and incubate (except in scrub-robins where males share more), with males feeding incubating females; both sexes provision young; incubation 14-20 days, fledging 12-22 days. Systematics: Part of basal passerid oscines, likely sister to Passerida or other groups like Eupetidae, Picathartidae, and Chaetopidae, with historical misalliance to Muscicapidae.

provenance.exact_quote: These upright-postured insectivores of Australasia frequent forests and forest edges. With their compact shapes, large round heads, and plumages of grays, browns, and blacks above contrasting with yellow, red, or even pink on the underparts, many Australasian robins recall their European namesake. Generally quiet birds, they sit and wait, often from a low perch only a meter or two above the forest floor, for passing insect prey. This group includes the ground-and scrub-robins, birds more terrestrial than the rest, and the latter distinctive for the long tails that they cock over their backs. Australasian robins live in a variety of wooded habitats, from dense tropical rainforest to open arid woodland and desert scrub and from sea level to high mountains. Some species, especially those in Australia, live in edge habitats near fields and grasslands. Petroicids are primarily insectivorous, though some species take substantial numbers of crabs and even small vertebrates, and others a good deal of fruit. Most species in the family pounce on their insect prey on the ground from a low open perch. But even the pouncing species will capture flying insects by sallying from a perch or by fluttering up to glean them from surrounding vegetation. The scruband ground-robins take all or most of their prey while foraging on the ground, grabbing visible prey or turning over leaves to search for them. All members of this family are monogamous with biparental care. Australasian robins maintain long-term pair bonds, and some species are cooperative breeders. Species that breed cooperatively usually have only one or two helpers at the nest. Nest shape is variable. Some (Microeca) are flat and very small saucer-shaped nests of grass and rootlets bound with spiderwebs. Most are open cups built of small twigs, rootlets, and vine tendrils, held together with cobwebs and decorated with moss and lichens, which sometimes hang from the bottom of the nest. Most species place their nests in a fork or on a branch, but the ground-and scrub-robins place their large bowl-shaped nests of sticks on the ground against a rock or tree trunk, and a few species nest in tree cavities. Female petroicids generally lay 1 to 3 eggs, although clutches of up to 6 have been recorded in some species. Except in the scrub-robins, where males take a more equal role in parental care, only the female builds the nest and incubates the eggs, although the male will feed her while she is incubating. Both sexes provision the young. In cooperative breeders, helpers also feed the female during nest construction and incubation, as well as provision the young. Incubation takes 14 to 20 days; the young leave the nest after 12 to 22 days and they are fed for some time after. Petroicidae is part of the group of loosely allied oscine passerines that we informally call the “basal passerid oscines,” which together are likely sister to the large and diverse Passerida (Barker et al. 2004, Jønsson et al. 2007, Irestedt & Ohlson 2008, Norman et al. 2009, Aggerbeck et al. 2014, Barker 2014). The Australasian robins were long thought to be allied with Muscicapidae, though molecular phylogenetic studies have suggested instead that they may be sister to the rest of Passerida (Barker et al. 2004, Beresford et al. 2005, Shepherd & Lambert 2007, Jønsson et al. 2011, Aggerbeck et al. 2014), sister to Eupetidae, Picathartidae, and Chaetopidae together (Jønsson et al. 2007), or sister to Notiomystidae, and presumably its sister family, Callaeidae (Barker 2014).
